A2: I coach software engineers who've just been made managers and are quietly drowning — I help them stop doing everyone else's job and start doing their own.
A5: Bristol, but the work is about 90% Zoom now — clients all over the UK plus a couple in Dublin. I run one in-person workshop a quarter at a co-working space near Temple Meads.
B4: Almost all of it is the 1:1 packages, and most of those come from referrals — ex-clients tipping off the next engineer who gets promoted at their old company. The newsletter converts a slow trickle. LinkedIn posts get lovely comments and roughly zero bookings.
C1: Dan, 31, senior backend engineer at a mid-size fintech in Leeds, promoted to team lead in March with a pay bump and precisely zero training. Still the best coder on the team and secretly proud of it, which is exactly the problem. Buys management books on the train and finishes none of them. Found me at 1am googling something like 'am I a bad manager or is my team just difficult' after his first direct report handed in notice. His company would probably pay for coaching but he was too embarrassed to ask, so he paid himself and expensed half of it later.
C2:
honestly before our sessions I was rehearsing my own standups in the shower. Six weeks in I ran a genuinely difficult conversation without feeling sick, and the weird thing is my team seem to like me MORE now I've stopped pretending to have all the answers. (email, April)

You said 'your job isn't to be the best engineer in the room anymore, it's to make the room better' and I think about that line every single day. Best money I've spent on my career and my company paid half lol (text from Dev — he said I could quote him)

I cried a bit after session two. In a good way. Nobody had ever told me the panic was normal.
C3: It isn't delegation frameworks. It's the 2am certainty that they've been found out — that everyone is about to discover a great engineer got swapped for a rubbish manager. What they're actually buying is permission to stop pretending they're fine and to learn the job out loud.
C4: Usually one specific bad moment — a first 1:1 that goes off the rails, their strongest engineer resigning, freezing in a skip-level meeting. Or their partner points out they've been miserable since the promotion.
C5: Price, mostly — £1,800 stings when the company won't chip in. Then the 'is coaching a bit woo?' thing; engineers are allergic to anything that smells of hustle culture. And time: they're already drowning, so six more hours of anything feels impossible. Which is rather the point, but you can't say that in an ad.
C6: Anyone who wants me to fix their team instead of themselves. People shopping for a script to manage someone out when they've already decided to sack them — had one of those in 2023, never again. And very senior execs who book a session and then spend it explaining why coaching is nonsense.
C8: Management books they don't finish (three bought, half of one read). Their company's generic new-manager e-learning module. Asking their own manager for advice, who was usually never trained either. A couple tried therapy first, which helps with the panic but not the actual Tuesday-morning job.
D1:
Deep End 1:1 — £1,800, six sessions over three months — engineering managers in their first 18 months.
Lifeboat session — £250, single 90 minutes, for one specific fire (a resignation, a bad review, a restructure announcement).
Corporate cohort — £6,500, five managers over eight weeks, same material, company pays.
Half-day team workshop — £2,400, usually sold alongside a cohort.
D2: Cohorts are the most profitable by a mile, but Lifeboat sessions are the easiest sell — £250, low stakes, people book them straight off one newsletter issue. The 1:1 package sits in the middle and is the work I actually love.
D3: More corporate cohorts. Same material, five managers at once, the company pays without blinking, and the group format genuinely works better — they discover they're not the only one winging it. Plus it stops my income being a strict function of my calendar.
D4: If someone doesn't find it useful after the first two sessions, I refund everything except those two. Taken up once in four years. It should be on the website; it is instead in my head.
D6: I won't do 'performance coaching' that's really about building a paper trail to sack someone. And I turn down companies that want me to coach managers they visibly undermine — happens more than you'd think.
E1: Ledgerline Leadership (ledgerline.example) — the big corporate provider with the procurement-ready deck. Marcus Tate, a solo coach who posts on LinkedIn four times a day (marcustate.example). And Codecrest Academy's self-paced manager course, which isn't coaching but competes for the same training budget.
E2: Ledgerline takes the corporate deals because they have a sales team and I have a Notion page. Individuals I mostly lose to doing nothing — they wait, hoping it clicks on its own. Marcus gets the ones who want swagger; I am not that, on purpose.
E3: I was an engineering manager for nine years — I've actually done the job, run the redundancy conversations, shipped late, been the one crying in the stairwell. Most leadership coaches came up through HR or L&D. Engineers can smell the difference inside ten minutes, and it changes how honest they're willing to be.
E5: There's a two-person accountancy in Sheffield, Marram & Low, whose newsletter reads like a letter from a clever friend — no images, no buttons, one good idea a week. That's the bar. Most coaching marketing makes my skin crawl, which is probably something to unpack.
F2: About 1,400 subscribers. I email most Tuesdays — skipped three weeks in May when the cohort work stacked up and felt guilty the entire time. Opens hover around 48%, which people tell me is good?
F3: Instagram — six months of carousels that took hours each and got 11 likes, mostly from other coaches. £300 on LinkedIn ads that got clicks and zero bookings. A webinar with nine signups and four attendees, one of whom was my mum's neighbour.
F4: Referrals from past clients, full stop — probably 70% of bookings. The newsletter compounds slowly; people book after lurking for eight months. And one guest spot on The Standup Log podcast brought four clients in a fortnight, which taught me borrowed audiences beat building my own from scratch.
G1: Sign two corporate cohort contracts by the end of September and get the 1:1 waitlist back up to ten names.
G4: September promotion season — loads of engineers get bumped to manager after summer performance reviews, it's my January. Also I keep saying I'll rewrite the website in August, and have said so every August for three years.
H2: Marram & Low again, sorry to bang on about accountants. Spoke & Word, a bike shop near me whose handwritten window signs are funnier than most agency work. And my old CTO, Elena, who could deliver awful news so plainly you almost thanked her for it.

H3.never_use: empower, rockstar, 10x, thought leader, 'crushing it', journey (as a noun for everything), anything with a rocket emoji
H3.must_use: drowning, the deep end, 'the job you were actually promoted into' — and clients are engineers, never 'leaders'

H4: I over-explain, which you'll have noticed by now. Please don't make me sound slick — the entire point is that I'm the coach for people who are allergic to slick. If a sentence could appear on a hustle influencer's slide deck, cut it. Also I hate selling and it shows; anything that helps me talk about the work without feeling grubby is worth double.
